label: vectors & remaining exponents — verified against schema, tier-guarded, math-verified

widget.prompt: x^(1/3) = 2 says the cube root of x is 2. Slide the base to 2 and read base³ — that reverses the root.
widget.successFeedback: 2³ = 8, so x = 8. Raising BOTH sides of x^(1/3) = 2 to the power 3 undoes the fractional exponent — the widget shows the undoing directly: cube the 2 that the root already gave you.

widget.prompt: 3⁴ / 3⁶ simplifies to a single power 3^?. Chain through the subtraction.

numericErrors.feedback: 2 ignores the sign of the subtraction. Dividing means the SMALLER exponent's power cancels out of the larger, leaving a NEGATIVE remainder: 4 − 6 = −2.
−10 adds the exponents, which is the rule for MULTIPLYING powers. Dividing subtracts: 4 − 6 = −2.

widget.successFeedback: 4 − 6 = −2, so 3⁴ / 3⁶ = 3⁻². A negative result here is not a special case — it just means more 3's cancelled from the bottom than were on top, which is exactly what a negative exponent records.
widget.explorationFeedback: Step through the chain before checking — the sign of the answer is the whole point.

widget.prompt: A(1, 2) to B(4, 6) is a displacement of ⟨3, 4⟩. Land the sum there and read its length.
widget.successFeedback: Length 5, from 3² + 4² = 25. A displacement vector's magnitude is the straight-line distance between the two points — the Pythagorean theorem wearing a vector's clothes, since 3 across and 4 up is exactly a 3-4-5 right triangle.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of (3, 4) — keep extending the arrow.

widget.prompt: u = ⟨4, −2⟩ is already two copies of ⟨2, −1⟩. Land v so that u + v gives THREE copies total — at (6, −3).
widget.successFeedback: v = ⟨2, −1⟩, the third copy, lands the sum at (6, −3) — exactly 3⟨2, −1⟩. Scalar multiplication by 3 is nothing more than three copies added together; the widget shows the third copy landing on top of the two already there.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of a third full copy — the sum has not reached (6, −3).
widget.highFeedback: Past three copies — the sum has gone beyond (6, −3).

refusals.title: Factoring with the GCF
refusals.why: Asks for the greatest common factor of two coefficients (6 and 9; 10 and 15) — a numeric computation with no spatial or manipulable representation. Distinct from ep-04-02/03 (already converted via binomialAreaLab in S203P), which factor TRINOMIALS as a rectangle's area; this is monomial GCF extraction, a different pattern binomialAreaLab does not model. Refused.

refusals.title: Matrix-vector product, determinant & inverse, solving systems with matrices, composing transformations
refusals.why: CHECKED THE ACTUAL SEMANTICS, not just the engine name. matrixTransform's own donor (vec-05-02) shows what it verifies: ta/tb/tc/td name a TARGET TRANSFORMATION, and the learner drags where î and ĵ land to CONSTRUCT it — the graded quantity is 'does this basis-vector mapping match the named transformation', never a raw arithmetic output. These four lessons ask for a component of Mv, a determinant, or one entry of a matrix PRODUCT — arithmetic on a GIVEN matrix, which the engine's interface does not expose. Refused.

refusals.title: Sixteen calculus theorem-application lessons across five courses
refusals.why: Every one of these uses steppedReveal as its sole interactive surface, and every one teaches a THEOREM'S REASONING STRUCTURE (Rolle's, MVT, related rates as chain-rule application, differentials and relative error, L'Hopital's hierarchy of growth, u-substitution as chain-rule-in-reverse, arc length as a limit of hypotenuses, comparison and alternating-series tests) rather than a quantity that can be dragged, built or measured. Checked against every calculus engine already in the catalogue -- derivativeTrace (one named curve, slope or point read), secantSlope (average or limiting slope between two points), graphZoom (behaviour AT a point) -- none represents 'which hypothesis of a theorem fails' or 'why does this bound hold' as manipulable state. This is the same shape as the S203K triangle-centre and S203R composition/piecewise refusals: the thing being taught is the argument itself. Refused as a group; re-examine individually only if a reasoning-structure engine is ever built.

refusals.title: Direction Angles & Building Components
refusals.why: DISCOVERED BY THE SCHEMA GATE. vectorExplore's targetX/targetY are constrained to INTEGERS (the contract summary I read did not surface the .int() modifier). The lesson's answer, tan(theta)=sqrt(3) at theta=60 degrees, requires landing at y=sqrt(3) -- irrational, and no integer y gives EXACTLY 60 degrees (tan 60 is irrational by definition), so there is no honest nearby grid point the way lg-04-01 substituted 2.7 for e. Refused.
